content.text:
Yes, H1 explains the data: one planet near 15.3 days brings the scatter under the limit and leaves no significant periodic signal behind.

**Best fit: F1** (from H1, period allowed to move ±10%)

| Quantity | Value | Judged against |
|---|---|---|
| Period | 15.312 d (started at 15.157 d) | Within the ±10% search range, not stuck on a bound |
| Semi-amplitude K | 78.9 m/s | About 191 times the noise level (K/σ√N), so the detection is very strong |
| Eccentricity | 0.092 | Nearly circular, not flagged as extreme |
| Scatter (RMS) | 2.43 m/s | Limit 3.91 m/s, so it **passes** |
| Reduced χ² | 0.94 | About 1 means the fit matches the measurement errors |
| BIC | 396.2 | Lower is better; 41,375 lower than the no-planet model |
| Flags | None | |

The fitted period ended up about 1% (0.155 d) longer than the starting value. That fits the earlier note that the 33.5-day baseline only loosely constrains the period.

**Residual periodicity:** the strongest leftover peak is at 2.34 d, with a false-alarm probability of 0.27, far above the 1% threshold. The other peaks (1.33 d, 1.95 d, 1.15 d, 6.28 d, 3.49 d) have false-alarm probabilities between 0.76 and 0.999, so they are noise. The 9.34 d peak that H2 is built on does not show up in the top six residual peaks. Together with the passing scatter, that gives no support for a second planet, though the PI should make the final call by comparing BIC with H2's fit.
